extracted.intended_audience: labor-law practitioners, employers, unions, NLRB stakeholders, and administrative-law commentators
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and standards for determining joint-employer (and related single-employer/employee) status under the National Labor Relations Act, comparing common-law agency tests, circuit approaches, and the NLRB's rule provisions (e.g., §103.40).

rubrics_metrics.name: Common-law master-servant/agency test for employee status
rubrics_metrics.description: When Congress uses the term 'employee' without definition, courts assume Congress intended the conventional master-servant relationship as understood by common-law agency doctrine.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cases cited: NLRB v. Town & Country Electric, Inc., Clackamas Gastroenterology Assocs. v. Wells, Nationwide Mutual Ins. Co. v. Darden, Community for Creative Non-Violence v. Reid, and others. The common-law inquiry emphasizes the 'right to control' the manner and means of performance; many sources use the terms 'master' and 'servant.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Single-employer four-factor test
rubrics_metrics.description: Single-employer analysis considers interrelation of operations, common management, centralized control of labor relations, and common ownership.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: From Radio & Television Broadcast Technicians Local Union 1264 v. Broadcast Service of Mobile, Inc.; used to assess when two entities should be treated as a single employer (distinct from joint-employer inquiry).

rubrics_metrics.name: Joint-employer 'share or codetermine' standard
rubrics_metrics.description: A standard asking whether two or more entities 'share or codetermine' control over essential terms and conditions of employment — historically understood as a shared 'exert[ion]' of 'significant control' over employees.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cited origins: Third Circuit's articulation in NLRB v. Browning-Ferris Industries of Pennsylvania, Inc. and subsequent case law. The final rule incorporates a 'share or codetermine' formulation in Sec. 103.40(b), but the interpretation (e.g., inclusion of indirect control or reserved authority) is contested.

rubrics_metrics.name: Actual exercise versus reserved (never-exercised) authority
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether an entity's unexercised contractual reservation of authority to control employees can, by itself, establish joint-employer status versus requiring actual exercise of control.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text records divergent authorities: some cases (and the D.C. Circuit in some contexts) treat the right to control as determinative even if not exercised; others require evidence of actual exercise or focus primarily on exercised control. The 2020 Rule's 'actual-exercise' requirement was criticized as inconsistent with common-law agency by some, but the Board also concluded that the 2020 rule's actual-exercise requirement was impermissible. The final rule and courts differ on how to treat never-exercised contractual rights.

rubrics_metrics.name: Direct and immediate control versus indirect control (including intermediaries)
rubrics_metrics.description: Distinction between control that is 'direct and immediate' and control that is 'indirect' (for example, control exercised through an intermediary such as a supervisor employed by the undisputed employer).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Debate over characterization: some courts/Board language treat intermediary-mediated control as indirect (and sometimes insufficient alone), while others (D.C. Circuit and some precedents) view control through intermediaries as 'indirect control' that nonetheless may be probative; the 2020 Rule and commenters differ on whether indirect control should be equated with direct control. The majority declined to provide examples of indirect control beyond intermediaries, leaving case-by-case development.

rubrics_metrics.name: Essential terms and conditions of employment (closed set approach)
rubrics_metrics.description: Focus the joint-employer inquiry on a (closed) set of 'essential' terms and conditions of employment necessary to permit 'meaningful collective bargaining.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The final rule adopts a closed list of essential terms (see Sec. 103.40(b)/(c)), and treats certain matters (e.g., work directions and discipline) as essential. The dissent argues that closing the list and declaring certain terms 'essential' may not satisfy the D.C. Circuit's call for legal scaffolding and may conflict with historical applications of the 'share or codetermine' standard.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exclusion of immaterial/control-over-routine-business-contracted-matters (§103.40(f))
rubrics_metrics.description: Evidence that an entity controls matters immaterial to a common-law employment relationship or that do not bear on employees' essential terms and conditions is not relevant to the joint-employer determination.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sec. 103.40(f) of the final rule provides that such immaterial evidence is irrelevant. Critics say §103.40(f) is largely the inverse of §103.40(a)/(b) and offers limited additional guidance to distinguish relevant indirect control from routine contracting terms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Independent-contractor factors (multi-factor test)
rubrics_metrics.description: Twelve-factor test used in some employee/independent-contractor analyses: (1) skill required; (2) source of tools/instrumentalities; (3) work location; (4) relationship duration; (5) right to assign additional projects; (6) hired party's discretion over when/how long to work; (7) method of payment; (8) role in hiring/paying assistants; (9) whether work is part of hiring party's regular business; (10) whether hiring party is in business; (11) provision of employee benefits; (12) tax treatment of the hired party.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The opinion notes these factors commonly appear in independent-contractor inquiries but explains they may have limited utility in joint-employer contexts because independent-contractor cases typically involve control exercised by the sole putative employer (hiring, paying), whereas joint-employer questions involve multiple entities and different evidence patterns.

rubrics_metrics.name: Circuit-specific formulations of joint-employer inquiry
rubrics_metrics.description: Different federal circuits apply varied, non-identical approaches to joint-employer questions (e.g., First Circuit 15 factors with emphasis on control over manner/means; Second Circuit asks whether entities 'share significant control' via 13 non-exhaustive factors; Third Circuit focuses on who paid/hired/fired and control over daily activities; Fifth Circuit applies a hybrid test emphasizing right to hire/fire/supervise/set schedules and which entity paid/withheld/provided benefits).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text summarizes recent circuit cases (Hurst; Felder; Perry; Faush; etc.) and emphasizes that circuit authority is not uniform, which affects how joint-employer status is assessed in different jurisdictions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Requirement to distinguish relevant indirect control from routine company-to-company contracting (D.C. Circuit mandate)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Board must explain the difference between indirect control that bears on the joint-employer inquiry and indirect control that reflects routine aspects of company-to-company contracting and therefore should carry no weight.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The D.C. Circuit remanded Browning-Ferris to require the Board to provide limiting principles; the opinion stresses that simply labeling control 'indirect' is insufficient without explaining why certain indirect controls matter to joint-employer status while similar contractual or commercial arrangements do not.

rubrics_metrics.name: Board discretion and policy considerations in setting the joint-employer standard
rubrics_metrics.description: Even within common-law bounds, the Board may exercise discretion for policy reasons to adopt a standard that excludes entities that have never exercised control over another employer's employees.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The dissent notes the Board has the policy authority (consistent with Sec. 1 of the Act) to adopt a rule aligning statutory rights/obligations with authority to control employees' essential terms; the Board is not compelled by the Act to adopt the broadest common-law possible formulation and may limit joint-employer status for sound policy reasons.

rubrics_metrics.name: Retroactivity and manifest injustice standard
rubrics_metrics.description: When adopting or refining a joint-employer standard, the Board may decline retroactive application if applying it retroactively would be 'manifestly unjust.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: On remand in BFI the Board found retroactive application of a refined standard would be manifestly unjust and dismissed the complaint and amended a certification; later court review vacated that retroactivity analysis. The point: retroactivity is a separate equitable consideration the Board may address.
